A variant's propositions and every statement about them, from a full bundle (clinvar-gkm_00-latest.json.gz, from Monthly Full Bundles):

uvx gkm-bundle-parquet@2.0.0 select --full clinvar-gkm_00-latest.json.gz "${P[@]}" \
    --driver variation --ids clinvar:10,clinvar:51592 \
    --follow in --max-depth 2 \
    --out two-variants.json.gz

--follow in from a variant reaches its propositions (depth 1) and the SCV, VCV and RCV statements about them (depth 2). To add what those statements point to (submitters, conditions, the VRS records), run a second selection from the statements with --follow out, for example --driver vcv --ids-file vcv-ids.txt --follow out.

Run on this laptop against the 2026-11 monthly (4.9 GB): 11 min, two passes over the file, under 100 MB of memory, 336 records. A selection streams the bundle, so it needs neither the memory nor the disk of a full build.
path: Build Your Own Tables and Mini-Bundles

items.title: One gene's variants
items.text:
The gene list on each variant points to gene, so --follow in from a gene reaches its variants, then their propositions, then the statements:

uvx gkm-bundle-parquet@2.0.0 select --full clinvar-gkm_00-latest.json.gz "${P[@]}" \
    --driver gene --where "name = 'MYH7'" \
    --follow in --max-depth 3 \
    --out myh7.json.gz

This is a full-bundle example, and it was not run for this page on a full bundle. A weekly delta holds only the genes whose records changed: the 2026-11-15 delta holds five, and MYH7 isn't one of them, so on the delta this command stops with no driver keys. With one of the delta's genes, --where "name = 'TMEM266-AS1'", the same command selects the gene and the 3 changed variants that point to it, in 1 s.
path: Build Your Own Tables and Mini-Bundles

items.title: Rows of one table
items.text:
--max-depth 0 follows no references, so a selection is a plain filter on the driver table. --where reaches into STRUCT columns by their dotted path. Every SCV classified Pathogenic in the delta:

uvx gkm-bundle-parquet@2.0.0 select --full clinvar-gkm-delta_2026-1115.json.gz "${P[@]}" \
    --driver scv --where "classification.name = 'Pathogenic'" \
    --max-depth 0 \
    --out pathogenic-scvs.json.gz

selected 2242 record(s) in 1 section(s) from clinvar-gkm-delta_2026-1115.json.gz: pathogenic-scvs.json.gz (491629 bytes, sha256 2253d30d…)
  scv                                          2242

2 s, 0.45 GB peak memory. The result is a bundle with one section; validate passes it.
path: Build Your Own Tables and Mini-Bundles

items.title: Tables straight from a selection
items.text:
build takes the same options and builds the selection's tables directly:

uvx gkm-bundle-parquet@2.0.0 build --full clinvar-gkm-delta_2026-1115.json.gz "${P[@]}" \
    --driver submitter --where "name = 'ClinGen Leukodystrophy and Leukoencephalopathy Variant Curation Expert Panel, ClinGen'" \
    --follow both --max-depth 3 \
    --out leukodystrophy-ep/

3 s, 0.3 GB peak memory, 264 KB of tables. Every file records the selection in its key-value metadata (gkm_bundle_parquet.selection), and so does manifest.json. verify --bundle-recompute checks such a set against its mini-bundle. rebuild refuses a set built with --driver; to get tables you can rebuild from, select the mini-bundle first and build --full it.
path: Build Your Own Tables and Mini-Bundles

items.title: Rebuild the bundle
items.text:
rebuild turns a full set of tables back into a bundle:

uvx gkm-bundle-parquet@2.0.0 rebuild parquet/ -o rebuilt.json.gz

rebuilt rebuilt.json.gz: bundle schema 1.2.0, 14 section(s), 39062 records, 68660443 bytes of text, records sha256 473016fd65cf2b61a81c04487597fa6f4b2a6cdea71ee694a14e6b518cb66927 (matches the manifest's records_sha256 and every section's section_records_sha256: record-identical to the source)

5 s, 0.7 GB peak memory, a 4 MB bundle. It needs every table, manifest.json and table-spec.json, but neither the schema nor the source bundle. Record-identical means each rebuilt record has the same canonical JSON as its source record: keys sorted, arrays compared as sets of values, numbers by value. The file's text differs (key order, spacing); the records don't. The records sha256 is a hash over every record's canonical form, which anyone can recompute from a bundle with a JSON parser and sha256; the tool's round-trip.md defines it.
path: Build Your Own Tables and Mini-Bundles

items.title: Verify a set of tables
items.text:
uvx gkm-bundle-parquet@2.0.0 verify parquet/
uvx gkm-bundle-parquet@2.0.0 verify parquet/ --roundtrip --full clinvar-gkm-delta_2026-1115.json.gz
uvx gkm-bundle-parquet@2.0.0 verify parquet/ --bundle-recompute --full clinvar-gkm-delta_2026-1115.json.gz "${P[@]}"

The first checks the directory alone, the second rebuilds the records and compares them with the bundle's, and the third recomputes every value from the bundle:

verify pass: directory check: 0 problem(s)
verify pass: directory check: 0 problem(s); round trip: identical
verify pass: directory check: 0 problem(s); bundle recompute: 0 group(s) differ
Check What it proves Delta verify DIR every file matches the manifest's sha256 and row counts, and carries the expected metadata < 1 s --roundtrip the tables rebuild the bundle's records exactly 6 s, 0.7 GB --bundle-recompute every row and value equals what the bundle gives 1 s, 0.2 GB

This is how the published set is checked before each upload, and how you can check a downloaded copy against the bundle of the same release. Add --report verify-report.md to any of the three to keep the result as a Markdown report, with a verify-report.json beside it.
path: Build Your Own Tables and Mini-Bundles

items.title: Validate a bundle
items.text:
validate checks every record against the bundle's JSON Schema, each record on its own:

uvx gkm-bundle-parquet@2.0.0 validate clinvar-gkm-delta_2026-1115.json.gz "${P[@]}"

bundle: clinvar-gkm-delta_2026-1115.json.gz (sha256 b370d385…, sidecar)
version: 1.2.0; schema set sha256 3b392018…
engine: rs; 10 workers
  section                                records  failing cpu ms/rec  compile s
  …
  scv                                     17,562        0      0.050        0.0
  vcv                                      2,941        0      0.069        0.0
  rcv                                      2,548        0      0.079        0.0
records: 39,062  failing: 0  (3.7 s)
PASS

4 s on the delta. --failures bad.jsonl writes each failing record's section, key and error paths. The default engine is jsonschema-rs; --engine python uses the GA4GH GKM Toolkit's validator instead (much slower; install gkm-bundle-parquet[reference]). Validate a bundle against its own schema_version's schema.
path: Build Your Own Tables and Mini-Bundles

items.title: See the columns before you build
items.text:
generate writes the column set the tables follow from, and lists every position the schema leaves as JSON text or as an IRI without a declared target:

uvx gkm-bundle-parquet@2.0.0 generate "${P[@]}" -o clinvar-gkm-1.2.0.columns.yaml

schema: "https://w3id.org/clingen/schema/clinvar-gkm/1.2.0/clinvar-gkm-bundle.schema.json"
version_property: "schema_version"
sections:
  sequenceReference: {type, name, extensions, refgetAccession, residueAlphabet, moleculeType}
  location: {id, type, digest, sequenceReference, start, end}
  allele: {id, type, name, digest, expressions, location, state}
  …

A column set you write yourself is a projection and must say projection: <name>. In 2.0.0 a projection can rename a column (name as submitter_name) and give a type to a position the schema leaves as JSON text, but it can't drop data: it must list every section, and the build stops on any record that holds a property no column covers. The 1.2.0 schema allows only what the pipeline writes, so a 1.2.0 column set has no column it can leave out. On the 2026-11-15 delta, leaving name out of submitter, and leaving the submitter section out, stop the build with:

error: table submitter: query failed: Invalid Input Error: table submitter: record: key clinvar.submitter:509533: top-level field(s) no column covers: [name]
error: schema …/1.2.0/clinvar-gkm-bundle.schema.json: section submitter: position (the record): the collection has no entry in the column set; the column set must list its properties

The 1.1.0 column set has fewer columns than its default only because the 1.1.0 schema allows properties no 1.1 bundle holds. See column-set-format.md. The published tables use no column set: they are the 1.2.0 schema's default.

To get fewer tables, build with --tables (Build the tables). To get fewer columns, build the tables and copy the columns you want into a file of your own with DuckDB, as in Materialize the joins you repeat (continues from Build the tables):

duckdb -c "COPY (SELECT id, classification.name AS classification, proposition FROM 'parquet/scv.parquet') TO 'scv-narrow.parquet' (FORMAT parquet)"

Such a file is yours to query; the tool's verify and rebuild don't read it.

Next: the 20 tables the default gives, and moving from the 1.1 tables.
path: Build Your Own Tables and Mini-Bundles

items.title: Joining Tables
items.text:
Release

Outputs on this page are from the 2026-10-31 release, built with gkm-bundle-parquet 2.0.0. Whole-release counts were computed from the 2026-10-31 bundle, which the tables reproduce record for record; the query outputs come from tables built from a selection of that bundle that holds every record about the example variants. Re-run a query to get today's numbers.

The 20 tables connect in five places, the seams. Two are plain foreign keys. The other three hide the trap that causes most wrong answers: a column whose values point at more than one table. A _section column next to it names the table each value points at. Join just one branch and the rows for the others disappear without an error.

Every query on this page runs against downloaded files; the joins read the larger tables, which is too much for the live console. Each table name links to its entry in the column reference.

Prerequisites

The DuckDB CLI, tested with 1.5.4, run from a directory holding the tables from Downloads → Parquet Files. Between them the queries read variation, the four proposition* tables, condition, conditionSet, scv, rcv, vcv and evidenceLine: about 3.5 GB of the 4.6 GB set. Each query stands alone, and each finishes in seconds on a laptop; the heaviest, the whole-release count in Seam C, took 5 seconds and under 2 GB of memory with 4 threads on a 16 GB Apple M2 Pro.

items.title: Seam A · Variant → Proposition
items.text:
Every proposition has a subject, and every subject is a variation id: 28,192,371 references in 2026-10-31. One glob reads the four proposition tables as a single table; union_by_name = true lines up their different columns, and filename = true adds the file each row came from:

-- One variant, every proposition, from all four tables
SELECT v.id, v.name,
       regexp_extract(p.filename, 'proposition[A-Za-z]+') AS prop_table,
       p.type, count(*) AS propositions
FROM 'variation.parquet' v
JOIN read_parquet('proposition*.parquet', union_by_name = true, filename = true) p ON p.subject = v.id
WHERE v.id = 'clinvar:10'
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY propositions DESC, p.type;

id          name                                    prop_table                type                             propositions
clinvar:10  NM_000410.4(HFE):c.187C>G (p.His63Asp)  propositionPathogenicity  VariantPathogenicityProposition            80
clinvar:10  NM_000410.4(HFE):c.187C>G (p.His63Asp)  propositionClinvarCustom  ClinvarNotProvidedProposition              12
clinvar:10  NM_000410.4(HFE):c.187C>G (p.His63Asp)  propositionClinvarCustom  ClinvarOtherProposition                     5
clinvar:10  NM_000410.4(HFE):c.187C>G (p.His63Asp)  propositionClinvarCustom  ClinvarRiskFactorProposition                5

The trap

Reading propositionPathogenicity alone, the obvious table for "what is claimed about this variant", returns 80 of this variant's 102 propositions. It misses the risk-factor, not-provided and other claims, with no error. Read proposition*.parquet unless you mean only pathogenicity.

items.title: Seam B · Proposition → Condition or ConditionSet
items.text:
A proposition's object is in object, and object_section names the table it points at. Across all four tables, in 2026-10-31:

object_section Joins to References condition condition.id (clinvar.trait:<n>) 25,214,935 conditionSet conditionSet.id: an accessioned ClinVar TraitSet (clinvar.traitset:<n>) or a set minted for a VCV aggregate (clinvar.conditionset:vcv-<md5>) 2,977,423 therapy therapy.id 6 therapyGroup therapyGroup.id 7

Even a tumor type is not always a single condition: 32 propositionOncogenicity rows name a minted condition set. The 13 therapeutic-response propositions put their tumor type in conditionQualifier instead, which always names a condition. Join each branch on object_section, and LEFT JOIN so a lost row shows up as UNRESOLVED instead of vanishing:

-- Resolve an object id to a name: condition.name, or the set's members joined by ';'
WITH set_names AS (
    SELECT cs.id, string_agg(c.name, '; ' ORDER BY c.name) AS member_names
    FROM 'conditionSet.parquet' cs, unnest(cs.concepts) AS t(m)
    LEFT JOIN 'condition.parquet' c ON c.id = m.id
    GROUP BY cs.id
)
SELECT DISTINCT p.object, p.object_section,
    coalesce(c.name, sn.member_names, 'UNRESOLVED') AS condition_name
FROM 'propositionPathogenicity.parquet' p
-- CASE keeps each join an equi-join (fast); an AND in ON plans a nested loop
LEFT JOIN 'condition.parquet' c  ON c.id  = CASE WHEN p.object_section = 'condition'    THEN p.object END
LEFT JOIN set_names           sn ON sn.id = CASE WHEN p.object_section = 'conditionSet' THEN p.object END
WHERE p.object IN (
    'clinvar.trait:16789', 'clinvar.traitset:13451',
    'clinvar.conditionset:vcv-5f128f0653d9f37c2777f7f939c33528')
ORDER BY p.object_section, p.object;

object                                                     object_section  condition_name
clinvar.trait:16789                                        condition       not specified
clinvar.conditionset:vcv-5f128f0653d9f37c2777f7f939c33528  conditionSet    Breast-ovarian cancer, familial, susceptibility to, 2; Hereditary cancer-predisposing syndrome; not provided; not specified
clinvar.traitset:13451                                     conditionSet    Alzheimer disease; Familial porphyria cutanea tarda; Hemochromatosis type 1; Microvascular complications of diabetes, susceptibility to, 7; TRANSFERRIN SERUM LEVEL QUANTITATIVE TRAIT LOCUS 2; Variegate porphyria

The trap

JOIN 'condition.parquet' c ON c.id = p.object (an inner join to condition only) keeps 25,016,660 of the 27,981,342 propositionPathogenicity rows. The 2.96 million whose object is a set (10.6 %) silently disappear.

items.title: Expanding a set to its member names
items.text:
conditionSet.concepts is a list of {id, section} members, not names:

SELECT id, membershipOperator, array_to_string([m.id FOR m IN concepts], '; ') AS members
FROM 'conditionSet.parquet'
WHERE id = 'clinvar.traitset:13451';

id                      membershipOperator  members
clinvar.traitset:13451  AND                 clinvar.trait:222; clinvar.trait:3370; clinvar.trait:5535; clinvar.trait:9582; clinvar.trait:9587; clinvar.trait:9601

To get names, unnest the list and join each member to condition, as set_names does above. Two more things matter:

  • membershipOperator changes what the set asserts. AND means the members together (a TraitSet describing one patient presentation); OR means any of them (every set minted for a VCV aggregate is OR). Carry it as its own column next to the names.
  • A minted set can contain a TraitSet. 28,776 of the 95,455 minted sets list a clinvar.traitset: member (section = conditionSet), so expansion goes one level deeper than it looks. It never goes further; TraitSets contain only traits.

This version handles the nesting:

WITH m1 AS (                                   -- direct members
  SELECT cs.id AS set_id, cs.membershipOperator AS op, m.id AS member, m.section
  FROM 'conditionSet.parquet' cs, unnest(cs.concepts) AS t(m)
),
m2 AS (                                        -- a member that is itself a TraitSet -> its members
  SELECT m1.set_id, m1.op, coalesce(n.inner_id, m1.member) AS trait_id
  FROM m1
  LEFT JOIN (SELECT cs.id AS sid, m.id AS inner_id
             FROM 'conditionSet.parquet' cs, unnest(cs.concepts) AS t(m)) n
         ON n.sid = CASE WHEN m1.section = 'conditionSet' THEN m1.member END
)
SELECT m2.set_id, m2.op,
       count(DISTINCT c.id) AS traits,
       string_agg(DISTINCT c.name, '; ' ORDER BY c.name) AS member_names,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE c.id IS NULL) AS unresolved
FROM m2
LEFT JOIN 'condition.parquet' c ON c.id = m2.trait_id
WHERE m2.set_id = 'clinvar.conditionset:vcv-48e5fe986b5c30669858fd0b2177c4e6'
GROUP BY ALL;

set_id                                                     op  traits  member_names                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       unresolved
clinvar.conditionset:vcv-48e5fe986b5c30669858fd0b2177c4e6  OR      11  Alzheimer disease; Cardiomyopathy; Familial porphyria cutanea tarda; Hemochromatosis type 1; Hereditary hemochromatosis; Microvascular complications of diabetes, susceptibility to, 7; Neuroendocrine neoplasm; See cases; TRANSFERRIN SERUM LEVEL QUANTITATIVE TRAIT LOCUS 2; Variegate porphyria; not provided           0

That set has seven traits and clinvar.traitset:13451 as members; the TraitSet's six traits overlap two of them, so the set covers 11 distinct traits. Flattening like this is right for a label. If the meaning matters, keep the nested set as a unit, since its members are AND-ed within an OR set.

items.title: Seam C · Proposition → Statements (1 : 1)
items.text:
Each statement table (scv, rcv, vcv) has a proposition column, and a proposition has at most one statement: in 2026-10-31, 28,190,803 statements point at 28,190,803 distinct propositions. Treat the proposition as a side table of its statement.

proposition_section names the table that holds the proposition, so a query about one kind of claim reads one file. A query over every statement spans all four; join the glob:

-- Where every statement's proposition lives
WITH stmt AS (
  SELECT 'scv' AS tier, proposition, proposition_section FROM 'scv.parquet'
  UNION ALL SELECT 'rcv', proposition, proposition_section FROM 'rcv.parquet'
  UNION ALL SELECT 'vcv', proposition, proposition_section FROM 'vcv.parquet'
)
SELECT s.tier, s.proposition_section,
       count(*) AS statements,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.id IS NULL) AS unresolved
FROM stmt s
LEFT JOIN read_parquet('proposition*.parquet', union_by_name = true) p ON p.id = s.proposition
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY s.tier, statements DESC;

On the 2026-10-31 release:

tier  proposition_section               statements  unresolved
rcv   propositionPathogenicity          12,021,260           0
rcv   propositionClinvarCustom              77,089           0
rcv   propositionSomaticClinicalImpact       5,239           0
rcv   propositionOncogenicity                4,912           0
scv   propositionPathogenicity           6,838,781           0
scv   propositionClinvarCustom              38,806           0
scv   propositionOncogenicity                2,456           0
scv   propositionSomaticClinicalImpact       1,752           0
vcv   propositionPathogenicity           9,121,301           0
vcv   propositionClinvarCustom              70,294           0
vcv   propositionOncogenicity                4,865           0
vcv   propositionSomaticClinicalImpact       4,048           0

Each tier's four rows sum to its row count. The 1,568 other propositionSomaticClinicalImpact rows (the diagnostic, prognostic and therapeutic-response propositions) have no statement: they are reached through SCI evidence lines (evidenceLine.targetProposition).

The trap

Joining statements to propositionPathogenicity alone drops 43,014 SCVs, 87,240 RCV statements and 79,207 VCV statements: every non-pathogenicity germline call, every somatic clinical-impact call and every oncogenicity call.

The column-reference entry for scv lists what each statement carries. To query statements directly by their proposition's subject, object or qualifiers without repeating this join, materialize it once.

items.title: Seam D · Inside an aggregate
items.text:
A VCV (or RCV) accession is not one statement but a small tree. Each root statement (…-G-PATH) cites its level statements (…-G-PATH-CP, …-G-PATH-NOCP, …) through an evidence line, and each level statement cites the SCVs at that level. SCVs cite nothing.

The edge is hasEvidenceLines (statement → evidence-line ids) followed by hasEvidenceItems (evidence line → cited {id, section}). All three kinds of evidence line are in the one evidenceLine table; a VCV statement's lines have ids starting with VCV:

-- One aggregate group: what each VCV statement cites, and whether it counts
SELECT s.id AS statement,
       el.strengthOfEvidenceProvided.name AS counts_toward_call,
       count(*) AS cites,
       string_agg(CASE WHEN item.section = 'vcv' THEN item.id END, ', ' ORDER BY item.id) AS cited_statements
FROM (SELECT id, unnest(hasEvidenceLines) AS el_id
      FROM 'vcv.parquet' WHERE id LIKE 'VCV000000010.%') s
JOIN (SELECT id, strengthOfEvidenceProvided, unnest(hasEvidenceItems) AS item
      FROM 'evidenceLine.parquet' WHERE id LIKE 'VCV000000010.%') el ON el.id = s.el_id
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1, 2;

statement                     counts_toward_call  cites  cited_statements
VCV000000010.142-G-NP         Contributing            1  VCV000000010.142-G-NP-NOCL
VCV000000010.142-G-NP-NOCL    Contributing            4
VCV000000010.142-G-OTH        Contributing            1  VCV000000010.142-G-OTH-CP
VCV000000010.142-G-OTH-CP     Contributing            1
VCV000000010.142-G-PATH       Contributing            1  VCV000000010.142-G-PATH-CP
VCV000000010.142-G-PATH       Non-contributing        2  VCV000000010.142-G-PATH-FLAG, VCV000000010.142-G-PATH-NOCP
VCV000000010.142-G-PATH-CP    Contributing           46
VCV000000010.142-G-PATH-FLAG  Contributing            2
VCV000000010.142-G-PATH-NOCP  Contributing            8
VCV000000010.142-G-RF         Contributing            1  VCV000000010.142-G-RF-NOCP
VCV000000010.142-G-RF-NOCP    Contributing            1

The root …-G-PATH statement shows the aggregation rule at work. Its call comes from the highest level present, here -CP (criteria provided). The -NOCP SCVs and the flagged ones are cited but marked Non-contributing. Reading a variant's statements explains the levels and their precedence.

Filtering evidenceLine by the accession prefix as well as vcv is what keeps this fast: rows are sorted by id, so the filter reads only the row groups for that accession.

items.title: Seam E · Every SCV to its aggregate, in one pass
items.text:
You don't need to walk the tree to find which aggregate an SCV belongs to. Every VCV evidence line's id begins with its statement's id, so one pass over evidenceLine, keeping only the SCV items, gives every pair:

CREATE TABLE scv_vcv AS
SELECT regexp_extract(el.id, '^VCV[0-9]+', 0)                  AS vcv_accession,
       regexp_replace(el.id, '\.(non-)?contributing$', '')     AS vcv_statement_id,  -- keeps the level: -PG, -EP, -CP, …
       item.id                                                 AS scv_id
FROM (SELECT id, unnest(hasEvidenceItems) AS item
      FROM 'evidenceLine.parquet' WHERE id LIKE 'VCV%') el
WHERE item.section = 'scv';

SELECT * FROM scv_vcv WHERE vcv_accession = 'VCV000000010' ORDER BY vcv_statement_id, scv_id LIMIT 6;

vcv_accession  vcv_statement_id            scv_id
VCV000000010   VCV000000010.142-G-NP-NOCL  clinvar.submission:SCV000020169.9
VCV000000010   VCV000000010.142-G-NP-NOCL  clinvar.submission:SCV000245789.3
VCV000000010   VCV000000010.142-G-NP-NOCL  clinvar.submission:SCV000607203.6
VCV000000010   VCV000000010.142-G-NP-NOCL  clinvar.submission:SCV001749317.2
VCV000000010   VCV000000010.142-G-OTH-CP   clinvar.submission:SCV000227124.6
VCV000000010   VCV000000010.142-G-PATH-CP  clinvar.submission:SCV000219176.11

On the whole release this yields 6,881,795 pairs, exactly one per SCV: every SCV is cited by exactly one VCV level statement. Keep vcv_statement_id, not just the accession; its suffix is what tells a -CP submission from a -NOCP or -EP one. Swap VCV for RCV to map SCVs to RCV accessions.

A useful identity: a VCV accession's number is the variation id. VCV000000010 is clinvar:10, with no exceptions across all 9,200,508 VCV propositions.

items.title: Joins that lie
items.text:
Every one of these returns a plausible answer with no error. Check them first when a count looks low.

Columns that point at more than one table

Column Points at Dispatch on object on every proposition table condition, conditionSet, therapy or therapyGroup object_section proposition on scv, vcv, rcv one of the four proposition tables proposition_section variation.members[] allele, copyNumberCount, or copyNumberChange members[].section conditionSet.concepts[] condition, or a nested conditionSet concepts[].section evidenceLine.hasEvidenceItems[] an SCV, or another statement in the same tier hasEvidenceItems[].section

Join every branch, or at least count the rows that matched nothing.

The gene context is not the variant's genes

geneContextQualifier.name is a gene symbol, and symbols are not unique (BTBD8 names two NCBI genes), so join on its NCBI Gene number, 'ncbigene:' || geneContextQualifier.primaryCoding.code. The qualifier is filled in only on SCV propositions (6,843,043 of them) and is NULL on every VCV and RCV proposition, so filtering aggregates by it returns nothing. It names one representative gene per variant, chosen upstream, not the genes the submitter named (those are in its submittedGeneSymbols extension); see Gene context. To find a gene's variants, use the variant's gene list, which carries ncbigene: ids, as in the PubMed-ids-for-a-gene recipe.

Next: Recipes puts these joins to work on real questions.

items.title: Moving from the 1.1 Tables to 2.0
items.text:
Release

Sizes and row counts on this page are from the 2026-10-31 release for the 2.0 tables (built as schema 1.2.0) and the 2026-10-24 release for the 1.1 tables, the last set the 1.1 line published.

From release 1.2.0, the published Parquet is built by gkm-bundle-parquet 2.0.0 directly from the JSON bundle, and published at v1/1.2/parquet/. It replaces the set exported from BigQuery for the 1.1 line, at v1/1.1/parquet/. This page calls them the 2.0 tables and the 1.1 tables. The records are the same; the table layout is not. Every query written for the 1.1 tables needs a review, and most need small rewrites.

Prerequisites

  • DuckDB CLI, tested with 1.5.4. No extension is needed.
  • The 2.0 tables: download all 20 into one folder (Parquet Files → Download) and start duckdb in that folder. The queries name each table by its file name ('scv.parquet') and read the four proposition tables with the glob proposition*.parquet.
  • The 1.1 tables, for the queries marked -- 1.1 only: a copy you downloaded from https://data.clinvar-gkm.org/v1/1.1/parquet/ before that set was removed (see Timeline), in a folder of their own. It is no longer served. The set is 13.2 GB; scv.parquet and variation.parquet are 3 to 4 GB each.
  • uv, for the rebuild example only. It reads the whole 2.0 set and writes a bundle about the size of the published one (about 5 GB compressed).

items.title: Who is affected
items.text:
• Parquet users: yes. Two tables are gone, almost every column outside the statement classifications is renamed or reshaped, and the data column is gone. A query against the 1.1 tables fails on the 2.0 tables with a binder error (Referenced column "proposition_id" not found), not with wrong numbers, so a broken query is easy to find.
  • JSON bundle users: no. The bundle is the record, and the Parquet change doesn't touch it. The bundle changes in 1.2.0 (the narrowed schema profiles, and aggregate primaryCoding, strength and direction) are in the changelog.
  • Copies you already downloaded keep working. A 1.1 table on your disk is unchanged; it simply stops being refreshed.

items.title: What stays the same
items.text:
• One row per bundle record, one table per bundle section, named after the section (scv.parquet, variation.parquet, …). Every id is unchanged: clinvar:51592, clinvar.submission:SCV000056982.2, VCV000051592.122-G-PATH-CP and every other key is the same string in both sets.
  • The statement columns most queries use. scv, vcv and rcv keep classification, strength, quality and direction, read the same way (classification.name, classification.primaryCoding.code, quality.name). scv keeps description, contributions, reportedIn and specifiedBy, and every statement keeps proposition_section. condition keeps name, aliases, conceptType, primaryCoding and mappings. Columns are matched by name, so their changed order inside a STRUCT doesn't matter.
  • One dataset, overwritten every release, with a manifest.json beside it naming the release it was built from (Parquet Files).
  • DuckDB, pandas, polars, R and Spark read both sets the same way. Only column names and types change.

items.title: At a glance
items.text: 1.1 tables 2.0 tables Built by BigQuery EXPORT DATA from the pipeline's tables gkm-bundle-parquet 2.0.0, from the published bundle Published at v1/1.1/parquet/ v1/1.2/parquet/ Tables 22 20: one per bundle section Evidence lines evidenceLine (SCV), vcv_evidenceLine, rcv_evidenceLine evidenceLine, all three kinds Column names snake_case derived columns (proposition_id, subject_variant_id, location_id) the bundle's own property names (proposition, subject, location) data column (the record as a JSON string) on every table (value on therapy, therapyGroup) none: every property is a typed column, and the tables rebuild the bundle's records exactly References bare ids in typed columns; #/… pointers inside data bare ids, plus a <column>_section column where the target table varies Qualifiers flattened (gene_context_id, mode_of_inheritance, penetrance) whole STRUCTs (geneContextQualifier, modeOfInheritanceQualifier, penetranceQualifier) The four proposition tables one shared column schema each table has only the columns its propositions use; read them together with union_by_name = true Row order unsorted sorted by id Size 13.2 GB (2026-10-24) 4.6 GB (2026-10-31) Self-description manifest.json manifest.json, table-spec.json, and key-value metadata in every file

items.title: Which set do you have?
items.text:
Any one of these tells them apart:

  • manifest.json. The 1.1 set says "builder": "BigQuery export"; the 2.0 set says "builder": "gkm-bundle-parquet 2.0.0" and "table_spec_version": "2.0".
  • table-spec.json. Only the 2.0 set has one: the compiled table spec, with every column's type, derivation and foreign keys.
  • The files themselves. A 2.0 file carries key-value metadata under the prefix gkm_bundle_parquet.; a 1.1 file has a data column (or, for therapy and therapyGroup, key and value).
-- 2.0 tables: one row per entry (tool version, spec version, the bundle's schema version, sha256s, ...)
-- 1.1 tables: no rows
SELECT decode(key) AS key, decode(value) AS value
FROM parquet_kv_metadata('scv.parquet')
WHERE decode(key) LIKE 'gkm_bundle_parquet.%';

items.title: Timeline
items.text:
When 1.1 tables (v1/1.1/parquet/) 2.0 tables (v1/1.2/parquet/) Until 1.2.0 is published the published set (built from 2026-10-24, not rebuilt since) not published When 1.2.0 is published: v1/1.2/ starts and v1/1.1/ is frozen kept, not rebuilt, until the 2.0 set is published empty until the set built from the newest 1.2 release is published, shortly after Once the 2.0 set is published removed: a frozen line keeps no Parquet (ADR 0008) the one published set, rebuilt every release
  • The live console on Start Here reads the current line's Parquet, so from the moment 1.2.0 is published it reads v1/1.2/parquet/. It has no tables to read for the short time until the 2.0 set is published.
  • The 1.1 tables are no longer served: they were removed once the 2.0 set was published, and they are not rebuilt, because they came from BigQuery, not from the bundle. A copy downloaded earlier still works with the -- 1.1 queries.
  • To get tables for an earlier release, build them from that release's bundle with gkm-bundle-parquet (see Build Your Own and Earlier releases). The columns come from the bundle's schema, so a bundle of schema 1.1.0 gives a wider set than the one this documentation describes, with more positions kept as JSON text; a bundle of schema 1.2.0 gives exactly these tables. For the 1.1 line, build with ClinVar-GKM's 1.1.0 column set instead: Parquet for Previous Releases.

items.title: Tables: 22 become 20
items.text:
Twenty tables keep their name. Two are gone:

1.1 table 2.0 table Rows evidenceLine (SCV evidence lines, somatic clinical impact only) evidenceLine, ids clinvar.submission:SCV… 1,568 in 1.1 vcv_evidenceLine evidenceLine, ids VCV… 9,376,374 in 1.1 rcv_evidenceLine evidenceLine, ids RCV… 12,157,527 in 1.1 one evidenceLine table 21,620,159 in 2.0

The bundle has always held all three kinds in its one evidenceLine section; only the 1.1 tables split them. See Evidence lines are one table.

items.title: Column by column
items.text: Every 1.1 column, and where it is in the 2.0 tables. A 2.0 column not listed is new. Gone means the column has no 2.0 counterpart because what it held is in other columns. Generated from the published 1.1 footers and the 2.0 table spec, then checked by hand.

items.title: Every table
items.text: 1.1 2.0 data (the record as a JSON string) gone: every property is a typed column; see No data column #/… pointers inside data bare ids in the typed columns, as before, plus <column>_section where the target varies a Coding's iris as VARCHAR[] (condition.primaryCoding.iris, every mappings[].coding.iris) STRUCT(id, section)[]: read iris[1].id

items.title: Variant tables
items.text: Table 1.1 2.0 variation members (VARCHAR[]) members (STRUCT(id, section)[]): m.id is the VRS id, m.section its table (allele, copyNumberCount, copyNumberChange) variation extensions[].value_hgvs_array extensions[].value_object_array on the clinvarHgvsList element variation extensions[].value_gene_array extensions[].value_object_array on the clinvarGeneList element; .gene is still a bare ncbigene: id variation extensions[].value_boolean, value_coding gone: no variation extension has those kinds variation constraints[].allele, constraints[].location the same names, plus allele_section, allele_json, location_section, location_json allele location_id location allele data->'$.expressions', data->'$.state' expressions (STRUCT(syntax, value)[]), state (STRUCT(type, length, sequence, repeatSubunitLength)) copyNumberCount location_id location copyNumberChange location_id, copy_change location, copyChange location sequence_reference_id sequenceReference location loc_start, loc_end start, "end": end is a reserved word, so quote it location loc_start_min, loc_start_max, loc_end_min, loc_end_max start_min, start_max, end_min, end_max, with the same meaning sequenceReference refget_accession, molecule_type, residue_alphabet refgetAccession, moleculeType, residueAlphabet gene concept_type conceptType; new: type, primaryCoding (the NCBI Gene coding) and mappings (HGNC)

items.title: Condition and therapy tables
items.text: Table 1.1 2.0 conditionSet concepts (VARCHAR[]) concepts (STRUCT(id, section)[]): c.section is condition or conditionSet therapy key, value, concept_type id, gone, conceptType; new: type therapyGroup key, value, membership_operator, members id, gone, membershipOperator, concepts (bare therapy ids); new: type

items.title: Proposition tables
items.text:
1.1 2.0 subject_variant_id subject object_id object object_type object_section (the same values: condition, conditionSet, therapy, therapyGroup) condition_qualifier_id conditionQualifier, plus conditionQualifier_section; propositionSomaticClinicalImpact only gene_context_id 'ncbigene:' \|\| geneContextQualifier.primaryCoding.code gene_context_name geneContextQualifier.name submitted_gene_symbols the submittedGeneSymbols extension of geneContextQualifier (value_string_array); NULL, not an empty list, when there is none gene_context_source the geneContextSource extension of geneContextQualifier (value_string) mode_of_inheritance modeOfInheritanceQualifier.name; propositionPathogenicity and propositionClinvarCustom only penetrance penetranceQualifier.name; propositionPathogenicity and propositionClinvarCustom only

Qualifiers are STRUCTs gives the expressions as SQL.

items.title: Statement and evidence-line tables
items.text: Table 1.1 2.0 scv, vcv, rcv proposition_id proposition (proposition_section is unchanged) scv, vcv, rcv has_evidence_lines hasEvidenceLines vcv, rcv extensions[].value, classification.extensions[].value extensions[].value_string, classification.extensions[].value_string vcv, rcv classification without a coding classification.primaryCoding (code, system), new in schema 1.2.0 scv contributions[].date (DATE) contributions[].date (VARCHAR, YYYY-MM-DD): CAST(date AS DATE) for date arithmetic scv, evidenceLine extensions[].value_submitted_condition, value_submitted_condition_set extensions[].value_object, one STRUCT for both; a set's concepts are JSON text scv specifiedBy.extensions[].value_document_array specifiedBy.extensions[].value_object_array evidenceLine target_proposition_id targetProposition vcv_evidenceLine, rcv_evidenceLine evidence_items (VARCHAR[]) evidenceLine.hasEvidenceItems (STRUCT(id, section)[]; section is scv, vcv or rcv) vcv_evidenceLine, rcv_evidenceLine directionOfEvidenceProvided, strengthOfEvidenceProvided the same names, on evidenceLine

items.title: No data column
items.text:
The 1.1 tables kept each record twice: a few typed columns, and the whole record as a JSON string in data. The 2.0 tables give every property of the record its own typed column or STRUCT field, at any depth, and drop data. They lose nothing: gkm-bundle-parquet rebuilds the bundle's records from the columns alone, and the build checks every row against its source record before it writes the file.

What you read from data before is now a column:

-- The 1.1 tables had only data->>'$.state.sequence'
SELECT id,
       state.sequence AS alt,
       [e.value FOR e IN expressions IF e.syntax = 'gnomad'][1] AS gnomad
FROM 'allele.parquet'
LIMIT 3;

When you need JSON:

  • One column or STRUCT as JSON: to_json(classification), or json_object('id', id, 'name', name) for several columns. The result is JSON built from the columns: references are bare ids, not #/… pointers, extension values sit in their value_<kind> slot, and absent fields appear as null. It is not the bundle record.

  • The bundle's own records: read the bundle, or rebuild it from a full set of tables:

    # run from the folder that holds clinvar-gkm-parquet/, the 20 tables and manifest.json
curl -f -o clinvar-gkm-parquet/table-spec.json \
  "https://data.clinvar-gkm.org/v1/1.2/parquet/table-spec.json"
uvx gkm-bundle-parquet@2.0.0 rebuild clinvar-gkm-parquet/ -o rebuilt.json.gz

    rebuild needs every table and the manifest.json and table-spec.json beside them. It writes a bundle whose records are identical to the source's: the same canonical JSON once key order, array order and whitespace are set aside. It checks that against the records sha256 the build recorded, and stops if anything differs. verify --roundtrip does the same check without keeping the output; see Build Your Own for both, with measured runs, and the tool's round-trip notes.

Dropping data is most of the size difference. In the 1.1 tables, data (and value) took 7.8 GB, 59 % of the 13.2 GB set, and the typed columns about 5.3 GB. Most of the remaining difference is in the evidence lines: 1.17 GB across three 1.1 tables, 0.26 GB in the one 2.0 table. The whole 2.0 set is 4.6 GB, about 65 % smaller than the 1.1 set, although it holds a newer and slightly larger release.

items.title: Evidence lines are one table
items.text:
evidenceLine holds every evidence line, and the id says which kind a row is:

Id Kind Columns it fills clinvar.submission:SCV<n>.<ver> an SCV's line (somatic clinical impact submissions only) targetProposition, evidenceOutcome, directionOfEvidenceProvided, extensions VCV<…>.contributing, VCV<…>.non-contributing a VCV statement's line hasEvidenceItems, strengthOfEvidenceProvided, directionOfEvidenceProvided RCV<…>.contributing, RCV<…>.non-contributing an RCV statement's line the same

To read only one kind, filter on the id, or reach the lines from their statements, which is what the queries on Joining Tables do:

SELECT CASE WHEN id LIKE 'VCV%' THEN 'vcv'
            WHEN id LIKE 'RCV%' THEN 'rcv'
            ELSE 'scv' END AS kind,
       count(*) AS lines
FROM 'evidenceLine.parquet'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY kind;

hasEvidenceItems replaces evidence_items. Each item is {id, section}, so an item's table no longer has to be read from its id's prefix: section is scv, vcv or rcv.

items.title: References: bare ids and _section columns
items.text:
A reference column holds the bare id of the record it points to, named after the bundle property: allele.location, location.sequenceReference, a proposition's subject, a statement's proposition. Where the property can point into more than one table, a <column>_section column beside it names the table:

Column _section values proposition object condition, conditionSet, therapy, therapyGroup (object_section) propositionSomaticClinicalImpact.conditionQualifier condition, conditionSet (conditionQualifier_section) statement proposition the four proposition tables (proposition_section)

In a list, each element is one STRUCT(id, section): variation.members, conditionSet.concepts and evidenceLine.hasEvidenceItems. A list whose targets are all in one table stays a list of ids: therapyGroup.concepts, and hasEvidenceLines on the statements.

Dispatch on the _section column, not on the id's prefix. The equality-join advice is unchanged: fold the section test into the join key so DuckDB keeps a hash join.

SELECT p.id, p.object_section, coalesce(c.name, '(a condition set)') AS object_name
FROM 'propositionPathogenicity.parquet' p
LEFT JOIN 'condition.parquet' c
       ON c.id = CASE WHEN p.object_section = 'condition' THEN p.object END
LIMIT 5;

table-spec.json lists every reference column, with its target tables, under each table's foreign_keys.

items.title: The proposition tables no longer share one schema
items.text:
In the 1.1 tables, all four proposition tables had the same 14 columns, many always NULL. In the 2.0 tables each has only the columns its propositions can have: only propositionSomaticClinicalImpact has conditionQualifier, and only propositionPathogenicity and propositionClinvarCustom have modeOfInheritanceQualifier and penetranceQualifier. Read the four together with union_by_name = true, which fills a column a table lacks with NULL:

SELECT regexp_extract(filename, 'proposition[A-Za-z]+') AS prop_table,
       count(*) AS propositions,
       count(modeOfInheritanceQualifier) AS with_mode_of_inheritance
FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet', union_by_name = true, filename = true)
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY propositions DESC;

Without union_by_name, DuckDB takes the glob's columns from the first file, propositionClinvarCustom. The columns every proposition table has (id, type, subject, predicate, object, object_section, geneContextQualifier) read as before, but conditionQualifier is a binder error ("not found"), and reading modeOfInheritanceQualifier stops with a schema mismatch when the scan reaches a table without it. Every query in these pages passes union_by_name = true.

items.title: Qualifiers are STRUCTs
items.text:
A proposition's qualifiers are kept whole, as in the bundle, instead of being flattened into a few columns. These expressions give back each dropped 1.1 column:

SELECT id,
       'ncbigene:' || geneContextQualifier.primaryCoding.code AS gene_context_id,
       geneContextQualifier.name                               AS gene_context_name,
       [e.value_string_array FOR e IN geneContextQualifier.extensions
                             IF e.name = 'submittedGeneSymbols'][1] AS submitted_gene_symbols,
       [e.value_string FOR e IN geneContextQualifier.extensions
                       IF e.name = 'geneContextSource'][1]          AS gene_context_source,
       modeOfInheritanceQualifier.name                         AS mode_of_inheritance,
       penetranceQualifier.name                                AS penetrance
FROM 'propositionPathogenicity.parquet'
WHERE geneContextQualifier IS NOT NULL
LIMIT 5;
  • gene_context_id is NULL exactly where it was: the placeholder qualifier has no primaryCoding.
  • A proposition with no qualifier has a NULL STRUCT, so every field of it reads NULL.
  • submitted_gene_symbols is NULL where the 1.1 column held an empty list.
  • The mode-of-inheritance qualifier also carries its HPO coding, modeOfInheritanceQualifier.primaryCoding.code (HP:0000006 for autosomal dominant), which the 1.1 tables had only in data.

What a gene-context qualifier means is unchanged; see Gene context.

items.title: Extensions: one slot per kind of value
items.text:
An extensions column is still a list of STRUCT(name, value_<kind>, …), and each element still fills only the slot its value needs. The slots are now named by the value's JSON kind rather than its meaning:

Value 1.1 slot 2.0 slot a string value_string (or value on vcv, rcv) value_string a boolean value_boolean value_boolean a list of strings in data only value_string_array an object value_submitted_condition, value_submitted_condition_set value_object a list of objects value_hgvs_array, value_gene_array, value_document_array value_object_array

Pick the element by name, as before:

SELECT id,
       [e.value_object_array FOR e IN extensions IF e.name = 'clinvarGeneList'][1] AS gene_list
FROM 'variation.parquet'
LIMIT 3;

An extension nested inside another extension's value (an HGVS entry's nucleotideExpression.extensions, a condition set's concepts) is kept as JSON text, one string per element; read it with json_extract_string or ->>. gkm-bundle-parquet generate lists every position kept as JSON text.

items.title: Smaller changes that break queries
items.text:
• "end" needs quotes. location.end is a reserved word in SQL: write "end", or alias the table (l."end"). start, start_min, start_max, end_min and end_max need no quotes.
  • Dates are text. scv.contributions[].date is VARCHAR (2025-03-04). Text comparison and ORDER BY work as before, because the format is YYYY-MM-DD; CAST(date AS DATE) for date arithmetic.
  • Rows are sorted by id. Nothing in the 1.1 tables promised an order, but a query that relied on file order now sees id order. A filter on id reads only the row groups whose id range can match (usually one), because each row group's minimum and maximum id are in the footer.

items.title: Query rewrites
items.text: Each pair is a 1.1 query and its 2.0 equivalent. The 2.0 queries are the ones the other pages of this guide use.

items.title: A variant's propositions
items.text:
-- 1.1
SELECT p.type, count(*) AS propositions
FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet') p
WHERE p.subject_variant_id = 'clinvar:10'
GROUP BY ALL;

-- 2.0
SELECT p.type, count(*) AS propositions
FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet', union_by_name = true) p
WHERE p.subject = 'clinvar:10'
GROUP BY ALL;

items.title: A statement's proposition and condition
items.text:
-- 1.1
SELECT s.id, s.classification.name AS classification, c.name AS condition
FROM 'scv.parquet' s
JOIN read_parquet('proposition*.parquet') p ON p.id = s.proposition_id
LEFT JOIN 'condition.parquet' c
       ON c.id = CASE WHEN p.object_type = 'condition' THEN p.object_id END
LIMIT 10;

-- 2.0
SELECT s.id, s.classification.name AS classification, c.name AS condition
FROM 'scv.parquet' s
JOIN read_parquet('proposition*.parquet', union_by_name = true) p ON p.id = s.proposition
LEFT JOIN 'condition.parquet' c
       ON c.id = CASE WHEN p.object_section = 'condition' THEN p.object END
LIMIT 10;

items.title: A condition set's member names
items.text:
-- 1.1
SELECT cs.id, string_agg(c.name, '; ') AS members
FROM 'conditionSet.parquet' cs, unnest(cs.concepts) AS t(cid)
LEFT JOIN 'condition.parquet' c ON c.id = cid
GROUP BY cs.id
LIMIT 5;

-- 2.0
SELECT cs.id, string_agg(c.name, '; ') AS members
FROM 'conditionSet.parquet' cs, unnest(cs.concepts) AS t(m)
LEFT JOIN 'condition.parquet' c ON c.id = m.id
GROUP BY cs.id
LIMIT 5;

items.title: The SCVs behind a VCV statement
items.text:
-- 1.1
SELECT s.id AS vcv_statement, item AS scv_id
FROM (SELECT id, unnest(has_evidence_lines) AS el_id FROM 'vcv.parquet'
      WHERE id LIKE 'VCV000000010.%') s
JOIN 'vcv_evidenceLine.parquet' el ON el.id = s.el_id,
     unnest(el.evidence_items) AS t(item)
WHERE item LIKE 'clinvar.submission:%';

-- 2.0
SELECT s.id AS vcv_statement, item.id AS scv_id
FROM (SELECT id, unnest(hasEvidenceLines) AS el_id FROM 'vcv.parquet'
      WHERE id LIKE 'VCV000000010.%') s
JOIN 'evidenceLine.parquet' el ON el.id = s.el_id,
     unnest(el.hasEvidenceItems) AS t(item)
WHERE item.section = 'scv';

items.title: Gene context
items.text:
-- 1.1
SELECT gene_context_name, count(*) AS scv_propositions
FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet')
WHERE gene_context_id = 'ncbigene:7157'
GROUP BY ALL;

-- 2.0
SELECT geneContextQualifier.name AS gene_context_name, count(*) AS scv_propositions
FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet', union_by_name = true)
WHERE 'ncbigene:' || geneContextQualifier.primaryCoding.code = 'ncbigene:7157'
GROUP BY ALL;

items.title: A variant's VRS chain
items.text:
-- 1.1
SELECT v.id, a.id AS allele, l.loc_start, l.loc_end, sr.name AS sequence
FROM 'variation.parquet' v, unnest(v.members) AS t(member)
JOIN 'allele.parquet' a             ON a.id  = member
JOIN 'location.parquet' l           ON l.id  = a.location_id
JOIN 'sequenceReference.parquet' sr ON sr.id = l.sequence_reference_id
WHERE v.id = 'clinvar:51592';

-- 2.0
SELECT v.id, a.id AS allele, l.start, l."end", sr.name AS sequence
FROM 'variation.parquet' v, unnest(v.members) AS t(m)
JOIN 'allele.parquet' a             ON a.id  = m.id
JOIN 'location.parquet' l           ON l.id  = a.location
JOIN 'sequenceReference.parquet' sr ON sr.id = l.sequenceReference
WHERE v.id = 'clinvar:51592';

items.title: A variant's gene list
items.text:
-- 1.1
SELECT id, [g.gene FOR g IN e.value_gene_array] AS genes
FROM 'variation.parquet', unnest(extensions) AS t(e)
WHERE e.name = 'clinvarGeneList' AND id = 'clinvar:51592';

-- 2.0
SELECT id,
       [g.gene FOR g IN [e.value_object_array FOR e IN extensions
                         IF e.name = 'clinvarGeneList'][1]] AS genes
FROM 'variation.parquet'
WHERE id = 'clinvar:51592';

This 2.0 query, and the next, pick the extension with a list comprehension instead of unnest(extensions) in FROM. The unnest form still returns the same rows, but it expands every record's extensions before it filters: over a minute for this one variant, against a few seconds.

items.title: Therapies
items.text:
-- 1.1
SELECT g.key AS therapy_group, t.name AS therapy
FROM 'therapyGroup.parquet' g, unnest(g.members) AS u(tid)
JOIN 'therapy.parquet' t ON t.key = tid;

-- 2.0
SELECT g.id AS therapy_group, t.name AS therapy
FROM 'therapyGroup.parquet' g, unnest(g.concepts) AS u(tid)
JOIN 'therapy.parquet' t ON t.id = tid;

items.title: An SCV's submitted condition
items.text:
-- 1.1
SELECT id, e.value_submitted_condition.name AS submitted_condition
FROM 'scv.parquet', unnest(extensions) AS t(e)
WHERE e.name = 'submittedCondition'
LIMIT 5;

-- 2.0
SELECT id,
       [e.value_object.name FOR e IN extensions IF e.name = 'submittedCondition'][1] AS submitted_condition
FROM 'scv.parquet'
WHERE list_contains([e.name FOR e IN extensions], 'submittedCondition')
LIMIT 5;

The Recipes, Joining Tables and Working at Scale pages are written for the 2.0 tables throughout.

items.title: Beyond DuckDB
items.text:
Release

The expected answer is from the published Parquet of the 2026-11-15 release. The Python and Spark snippets were run against it with Python 3.14.5, DuckDB 1.5.4, pyarrow 26.0.1, pandas 3.1.1, polars 2.1.0 and PySpark 4.0.1 (OpenJDK 21). The R snippet was last run on the 2026-10-31 release, with R 4.6.1, arrow 26.0.1.1 and dplyr 1.2.1.

Parquet is an open format, so any tool that reads it can read these files. This page does the same small task in each, so you can compare them: count the expert-panel SCVs by normalized classification, reading only the two fields that needs.

The expected answer, whichever tool you use:

code                    n
pathogenic              10,078
uncertain significance   4,096
likely pathogenic        3,078
benign                   2,887
likely benign            2,873
…

Whatever the tool, the rule from Anatomy of a Table holds: read only the columns you need. scv.parquet is 785 MB on disk in 2026-11-15, and several times that once loaded whole.

Prerequisites

  • Data: scv.parquet (784 MB) in the directory you run from, from Downloads → Parquet Files; the spreadsheet example reads condition.parquet (2 MB). Each snippet stands alone and reads only two fields; the pyarrow and pandas ones peaked at about 1.4 GB of memory.

  • Python (tested with 3.14.5): install only the libraries for the snippets you run.

    python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install "duckdb==1.5.4" "pyarrow==26.0.1" "pandas==3.1.1" "polars==2.1.0"

  • R (tested with 4.6.1): install.packages(c("arrow", "dplyr")). Where CRAN has no binary for your R, as with Homebrew's R on macOS, arrow compiles from source: set Sys.setenv(NOT_CRAN = "true", LIBARROW_BINARY = "true") first so it downloads a prebuilt Arrow C++ library, and expect the install to take 15 minutes or more.

  • Spark (optional): Java 17 or 21 (tested with OpenJDK 21) and pip install "pyspark==4.0.1" (about 430 MB) in the same environment.
  • Command line: the DuckDB CLI, tested with 1.5.4.

items.title: DuckDB from Python
items.text:
The SQL on the rest of this track runs unchanged from Python, and .df() hands the result to pandas:

import duckdb

df = duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT classification.primaryCoding.code AS code, count(*) AS n
    FROM 'scv.parquet'
    WHERE quality.name = 'expert panel'
    GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC
""").df()
print(df.head())

Use this when the work is mostly joins and filtering: DuckDB does them out of memory, and only the small result becomes a DataFrame.

items.title: pyarrow
items.text:
pyarrow reads the schema and metadata from the footer, and can read individual fields out of nested columns. The footer also says what built the file: its key-value metadata has gkm_bundle_parquet.* entries such as tool_version and bundle_schema_version.

import pyarrow.parquet as pq
import pyarrow.compute as pc

pf = pq.ParquetFile("scv.parquet")                     # opening reads only the footer
print(pf.metadata.num_rows, "rows in", pf.metadata.num_row_groups, "row groups")
print(pf.schema_arrow.field("quality").type)
print(pf.metadata.metadata[b"gkm_bundle_parquet.bundle_schema_version"])

# Read two nested fields, not the whole table; they come back as columns "code" and "name"
t = pq.read_table("scv.parquet",
                  columns=["classification.primaryCoding.code", "quality.name"])
ep = t.filter(pc.equal(t["name"], "expert panel"))
print(ep.group_by("code").aggregate([("code", "count")])
        .sort_by([("code_count", "descending")]).slice(0, 5).to_pylist())

A dotted path in columns= reads just that leaf. Note that the result names the column by its last segment (code, name), not the full path.

items.title: pandas
items.text:
pandas reads Parquet through pyarrow, with the same columns=:

import pandas as pd

# columns= is essential: without it pandas loads every column of scv, decompressed
df = pd.read_parquet("scv.parquet",
                     columns=["classification.primaryCoding.code", "quality.name"])
print(df.columns.tolist())                               # ['code', 'name']
print(df.loc[df["name"] == "expert panel", "code"].value_counts().head())

Never pd.read_parquet a big table without columns=

It loads every column into memory, decompressed: several times the file's size on disk, most of it free text and extensions you didn't ask for. On the big tables the process is killed or the machine swaps.

items.title: polars
items.text:
polars' scan_parquet is lazy: it builds a query plan and, on .collect(), reads only the columns and rows the plan needs:

import polars as pl

out = (
    pl.scan_parquet("scv.parquet")                       # lazy: nothing is read yet
      .select(code=pl.col("classification").struct.field("primaryCoding").struct.field("code"),
              level=pl.col("quality").struct.field("name"))
      .filter(pl.col("level") == "expert panel")
      .group_by("code").len()
      .sort("len", descending=True)
      .collect()                                         # reads only the needed columns
)
print(out.head())

Use scan_parquet, not read_parquet: the eager read_parquet loads the file first, with the same memory problem as pandas.

items.title: R
items.text:
The arrow package opens a file as a dataset and translates dplyr verbs into a column-pruned scan; nothing is read until collect():

library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

open_dataset("scv.parquet") |>
  transmute(code  = classification$primaryCoding$code,
            level = quality$name) |>
  filter(level == "expert panel") |>
  count(code, sort = TRUE) |>
  collect()

The duckdb R package is the other route: it runs the SQL from this track unchanged.

items.title: Spark
items.text:
Spark reads the files as they are, with dotted access into the STRUCT columns. Locally, with PySpark:

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F

spark = (SparkSession.builder.master("local[*]").appName("clinvar-gkm")
         .config("spark.driver.bindAddress", "127.0.0.1")   # a laptop: bind the driver to loopback
         .config("spark.driver.host", "127.0.0.1")
         .getOrCreate())
scv = spark.read.parquet("scv.parquet")
(scv.where(F.col("quality.name") == "expert panel")
    .groupBy(F.col("classification.primaryCoding.code").alias("code"))
    .count()
    .orderBy(F.desc("count"))
    .show(5, truncate=False))
spark.stop()

+----------------------+-----+
|code                  |count|
+----------------------+-----+
|pathogenic            |10078|
|uncertain significance|4096 |
|likely pathogenic     |3078 |
|benign                |2887 |
|likely benign         |2873 |
+----------------------+-----+
only showing top 5 rows

Under 30 seconds on the test laptop, most of it starting Spark. The two config lines stop a laptop's Spark failing with Can't assign requested address: Service 'sparkDriver'; drop them on a cluster. On a cluster, read the files from your own storage (spark.read.parquet("s3://…/scv.parquet")).

items.title: BigQuery and other warehouses
items.text:
Copy the files into your own bucket first: data.clinvar-gkm.org is a download host, not a query endpoint for warehouse engines. For BigQuery, load each table from a Cloud Storage copy.

Not run here; needs a GCP project

These commands weren't run for this page. They need a Google Cloud project with billing, a Cloud Storage bucket and a BigQuery dataset of your own; loading and querying are billed to that project. Replace my-bucket and my_dataset.

gcloud storage cp scv.parquet gs://my-bucket/clinvar-gkm/scv.parquet
bq load --source_format=PARQUET --parquet_enable_list_inference=true \
    my_dataset.scv gs://my-bucket/clinvar-gkm/scv.parquet

--parquet_enable_list_inference=true makes a Parquet list a BigQuery ARRAY; without it, each list column arrives wrapped in an extra record (hasEvidenceLines.list.element). An external table over the same gs:// path (bq mk --external_table_definition) queries the files without loading them.

What survives the trip, in BigQuery, Spark and Athena alike:

  • STRUCT and LIST columns arrive as the engine's record and array types (STRUCT/ARRAY in BigQuery and Spark, struct/array in Athena), so dotted access like classification.name works the same way.
  • Every field is a typed column, except the few nested positions kept as JSON text (see Extensions); parse those with the engine's JSON functions (JSON_VALUE in BigQuery, get_json_object in Spark).
  • Ids are plain strings. The joins on Joining Tables translate directly, _section dispatch included.
  • Column names are camelCase (primaryCoding, hasEvidenceLines), as in the bundle. Some engines fold unquoted names to lower case; check how yours matches Parquet column names.

items.title: Spreadsheets and GUI tools
items.text:
Excel, Google Sheets and most GUI tools can't open Parquet, and even those that can shouldn't open a multi-GB table. Filter to the rows you need first, then export that slice to CSV:

duckdb -c "COPY (SELECT id, name FROM 'condition.parquet') TO 'conditions.csv' (HEADER)"

Recipes → Export a slice has a fuller example. With no terminal at all, the DuckDB Web Shell can open a small downloaded file in the browser and export the result.

items.title: Which tool when
items.text: For exploring and for joins, DuckDB, from the command line or from Python or R: it reads only what a query needs and handles joins larger than memory. For a dataframe workflow in Python, polars with scan_parquet gives the same column pruning with a dataframe API. Use pandas or pyarrow when a library you depend on expects their objects, and always pass columns=. Reach for Spark or a warehouse only when the data has to live next to other large data in your cloud. For everyone else, 4.6 GB of Parquet on a laptop is small.

items.title: Working at Scale
items.text:
Release

File and row-group sizes on this page are from a gkm-bundle-parquet 2.0.0 build of the 2026-10-31 release. The timings and peak memory in Materialize the joins you repeat were measured on 2026-11-21 against the published 2026-11-15 tables, with the DuckDB 1.5.4 CLI on an Apple M2 Pro laptop (16 GB of memory, 10 cores). Your numbers will differ with the release and your machine.

The 2026-10-31 tables total 4.6 GB. Eight are over 100 MB: variation (1.66 GB), scv (784 MB), allele (701 MB), location (427 MB), propositionPathogenicity (401 MB), evidenceLine (265 MB), rcv (182 MB) and vcv (145 MB). The other twelve are each 5 MB or less. A handful of habits keeps queries over the big ones fast on a laptop.

items.title: What you need
items.text:
Prerequisites

The DuckDB CLI, tested with 1.5.4, run from a directory holding the tables each example names, downloaded from Downloads → Parquet Files. The materialized tables need scv.parquet and the four proposition*.parquet tables (about 1.2 GB), about 3 GB of memory, 0.7 GB of disk for the database file and a little over a minute to build. The table below has the details.

DuckDB The files are written with DuckDB 1.5.4 (each file's gkm_bundle_parquet.duckdb_version metadata and the manifest's duckdb_version say so). The queries in this track were run with DuckDB 1.5.4, from the command line and from Python. Any reader with Parquet nested types (STRUCT, lists) reads the files; the SQL uses DuckDB syntax. Disk 4.6 GB for all 20 tables. Most questions need only a few: the column reference gives every table's size. condition, conditionSet, gene, submitter, therapy, therapyGroup and the three smaller proposition tables together are under 20 MB. Add room for DuckDB's spill files when a big join runs short of memory (see settings). Memory Depends on the query, not the file size: a query reads only the columns it names. Lookups and filters on one table need little. A join or GROUP BY across two of the big tables is the heavy case; DuckDB caps itself at 80 % of RAM and spills to disk past that, so it finishes on a laptop, more slowly. Loading a whole big table into pandas needs its full decompressed size, several times its size on disk. Python duckdb 1.5.4 and, for Arrow or pandas, pyarrow; see Working in Python for a tested set of versions. To build the tables yourself A full build needs far more: about 65 GiB of memory and 65 GB of working disk; see Build Your Own.

items.title: Name your columns
items.text:
Parquet stores each column separately, and a query reads only the columns it names. This is the single biggest lever you have. In scv.parquet, the free-text description and the extensions are most of the table, on disk and far more in memory (the breakdown). A query that names two small fields reads almost none of it.

To see where any table's bytes are, ask its metadata. This reads only the file footer:

SELECT split_part(path_in_schema, ',', 1)          AS col,
       round(sum(total_compressed_size)   / 1e6, 2) AS mb_on_disk,
       round(sum(total_uncompressed_size) / 1e6, 2) AS mb_in_memory
FROM parquet_metadata('scv.parquet')
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY mb_in_memory DESC;

The same holds for fields inside a STRUCT: classification.name reads that one field, not the whole classification record. Selecting * or the struct as a whole reads everything.

items.title: Look up by id
items.text:
Every table is sorted by id and written in row groups of up to 122,880 rows, each with the minimum and maximum id it holds. A filter on id (WHERE id = …, WHERE id LIKE 'VCV000000010.%') lets DuckDB skip every row group whose range can't match, so it reads one or two row groups instead of the whole file. That is what makes the evidence-line lookups in Seam D fast: filtering evidenceLine by an accession prefix reads one row group of about 176.

A filter on any other column (subject, object, name) can't skip anything, because those values are spread across the file. When you look up by such a column again and again, materialize a copy sorted by it.

items.title: Reach into nested lists without unnest
items.text:
Several columns are lists of records: variation.extensions, variation.members, scv.contributions, scv.reportedIn. To filter on something inside them, prefer a list comprehension, [x.field FOR x IN list IF …], over unnest. unnest turns every list element into its own row before filtering; a comprehension filters each list in place, which is many times faster on variation. The gene rollup recipe shows the comprehension.

Use comprehensions rather than lambda functions (list_filter(l, x -> …)). DuckDB 1.5 deprecates that arrow syntax, and the replacement (lambda x: …) is too new for the browser console's engine. Comprehensions work in both.

items.title: Join on a plain equality
items.text: DuckDB joins two big tables fast, with a hash join, when the ON clause is one equality between them. Add a second condition (ON p.object_section = 'condition' AND c.id = p.object), or join through a function (ON list_contains(…)), and DuckDB 1.5 plans a nested-loop join instead, which compares row against row and can run for hours on propositionPathogenicity. Fold the extra condition into the key, ON c.id = CASE WHEN p.object_section = 'condition' THEN p.object END, or unnest the list in a subquery and join on the plain column. Seam B shows the first; Find the variant shows the second. Put EXPLAIN in front of a query to check before you run it: HASH_JOIN is the fast kind; NESTED_LOOP_JOIN, BLOCKWISE_NL_JOIN and PIECEWISE_MERGE_JOIN are the slow kinds.

items.title: Local or remote
items.text:
DuckDB reads Parquet over HTTPS with range requests: it fetches the file's footer first, then only the byte ranges of the row groups and columns a query needs. That makes some remote queries as cheap as local ones and others impractical:

Over the network Requests Works? DESCRIBE, count(*), parquet_metadata(…) footer only yes, in about a second on any table LIMIT n without a filter footer + first row group yes A filter on id footer + the row groups whose range matches yes Any query on a small table (condition, gene, submitter, therapy, …) a few yes Any other filter, GROUP BY or join over a big table one per row group per column: about 56 row groups in scv, 228 in propositionPathogenicity, 176 in evidenceLine slowly, and a burst of requests can be refused; download for repeated or heavier work

The CDN in front of data.clinvar-gkm.org allows about 55 requests per 10 seconds per client and refuses more with HTTP 429 for a short time. The rule: query remotely to explore, download to analyze. Download the tables a question needs once (see Start Here), and the queries on this page and in Recipes run locally.

items.title: DuckDB settings for a laptop
items.text:
DuckDB's defaults suit most queries here: it uses every CPU core, caps itself at 80 % of RAM, and spills to a .tmp directory when a query needs more. When a big join or GROUP BY runs out of memory, you see this:

Out of Memory Error: could not allocate block of size 256.0 KiB (953.5 MiB/953.6 MiB used)

Possible solutions:
* Reducing the number of threads (SET threads=X)
* Disabling insertion-order preservation (SET preserve_insertion_order=false)
* Increasing the memory limit (SET memory_limit='...GB')

The suggestions are the right ones, in that order:

Setting Effect SET threads = 2; Each thread holds its own working memory; fewer threads means a smaller peak. SET preserve_insertion_order = false; Lets DuckDB skip buffering rows to keep them in file order. Use it whenever the result has an ORDER BY or order doesn't matter. SET memory_limit = '8GB'; Raises (or lowers) the cap. SET temp_directory = '/path/with/space'; Moves the spill files to a disk with room.

For work you repeat, open a database file (duckdb clinvar-gkm.duckdb) rather than an in-memory session. Tables you create there persist, which is what makes the next section possible.

items.title: Materialize the joins you repeat
items.text:
Statements and propositions live in separate tables. An SCV row holds its classification but not the variant or condition it is about. Those are on the proposition, in one of four tables with different qualifier columns. So any question about statements by subject (a variant), object (a condition, tumor type or therapy) or qualifier (gene context, mode of inheritance, penetrance) has to join two big tables first.

Paying for that join on every query is slow locally, and slower over the network: scv.parquet is sorted by SCV id and has no variant column, so a lookup for one variant must read every row group of the file. In the browser's live console it can also exhaust memory or trip the CDN's rate limit (HTTP 429).

The fix is to run the join once, store the result as a table sorted by the column you look up most, and query that table instead. DuckDB has no CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW; CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT in a database file does the same job. You refresh it by re-running the script when you download a new release.

items.title: Build it
items.text:
Download the four proposition tables and scv.parquet (see Start Here) into one directory. Save the SQL below there as materialize.sql, then run it from that directory. It writes a database file, clinvar-gkm.duckdb, that persists between sessions:

duckdb clinvar-gkm.duckdb < materialize.sql

On the test laptop (see the release note at the top) the build took 71 seconds with DuckDB's default settings, peaked at about 3 GB of memory, and wrote a 0.65 GB database file.

-- materialize.sql
SET preserve_insertion_order = false;   -- lets DuckDB build large tables with less memory

-- 1. One proposition table: union_by_name lines up the four tables' different qualifier columns.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE prop AS
SELECT id, type AS proposition_type, predicate,
       subject AS variant_id, object AS object_id, object_section,
       geneContextQualifier.name                    AS gene_context_name,
       'ncbigene:' || geneContextQualifier.primaryCoding.code AS gene_context_id,
       modeOfInheritanceQualifier.name              AS mode_of_inheritance,
       penetranceQualifier.name                     AS penetrance,
       conditionQualifier                           AS condition_qualifier_id
FROM read_parquet('proposition*.parquet', union_by_name = true);

-- 2. SCV statements with their proposition's subject, object and qualifiers inlined,
--    sorted by variant so a lookup by variant touches one small slice of the table.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE scv_by_variant AS
SELECT p.variant_id, p.object_id, p.object_section, p.proposition_type, p.predicate,
       p.gene_context_name, p.gene_context_id, p.mode_of_inheritance, p.penetrance, p.condition_qualifier_id,
       s.id                     AS scv_id,
       s.classification.name    AS classification,
       s.quality.name           AS submission_level,
       s.direction,
       [c.contributor FOR c IN s.contributions IF c.activityType = 'submitted'][1] AS submitter_id,
       [r.pmid FOR r IN s.reportedIn IF r.pmid IS NOT NULL]                        AS pmids
FROM 'scv.parquet' s
JOIN prop p ON p.id = s.proposition
ORDER BY p.variant_id, s.id;

Only the columns the questions below need are carried over. Add others, such as s.description or s.specifiedBy.name, the same way.

items.title: Query it
items.text:
Each of these reads one small, sorted table, where the same question against the raw Parquet files means a join of two big ones. Run them in the database the build wrote (duckdb clinvar-gkm.duckdb); each took under half a second.

By subject (a variant)

-- PubMed ids cited by the SCVs for one variant
SELECT pmid, count(*) AS n_scvs,
       string_agg(replace(scv_id, 'clinvar.submission:', ''), ', ') AS cited_by
FROM (SELECT scv_id, unnest(pmids) AS pmid
      FROM scv_by_variant WHERE variant_id = 'clinvar:10')
GROUP BY pmid
ORDER BY n_scvs DESC, pmid;

By object (a condition)

-- What submitters have called variants for one condition
SELECT classification, count(*) AS n
FROM scv_by_variant
WHERE object_id = 'clinvar.trait:9580'      -- Hereditary spastic paraplegia 48
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC;

This matches propositions whose object is that condition. A proposition about a condition set that contains it has a clinvar.traitset: or clinvar.conditionset: object instead. To include those, expand the sets as shown in Joining Tables.

By qualifier

-- Pathogenic calls made under autosomal recessive inheritance, by submission level
SELECT submission_level, count(*) AS n
FROM scv_by_variant
WHERE mode_of_inheritance = 'Autosomal recessive inheritance'
  AND classification = 'Pathogenic'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC;

items.title: The same pattern for the aggregates
items.text:
VCV and RCV statements join to the same prop table. Add this to materialize.sql (it needs prop and vcv.parquet; 14 seconds on the test laptop) to get every aggregate statement for a variant in one lookup:

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE vcv_by_variant AS
SELECT p.variant_id, p.object_id, p.proposition_type,
       v.id AS vcv_id, v.classification.name AS classification,
       v.quality.name AS aggregate_level, v.direction
FROM 'vcv.parquet' v
JOIN prop p ON p.id = v.proposition
ORDER BY p.variant_id, v.id;

For rcv, swap in rcv.parquet.

items.title: Share it as a sorted Parquet file
items.text:
A materialized table can go back out as Parquet. Run this in clinvar-gkm.duckdb, which holds scv_by_variant (about 3 seconds; a 122 MB file). Because the rows are sorted by variant_id, DuckDB's per-row-group min/max statistics let a reader skip almost all of the file, the same way the published tables skip by id:

COPY scv_by_variant TO 'scv_by_variant.parquet' (FORMAT parquet);

The same layout is what would make per-variant queries practical over the network, where every row group read is a request.

items.title: Errors that look worse than they are
items.text:
Parser Error: syntax error at or near "end": end is a reserved word, and location has a column named end. Quote it: "end". The same error with "name" means a column alias without AS: many words used as column names in these tables are reserved, so SELECT name name FROM 'condition.parquet' fails while SELECT name AS name … works. The same goes for type, value, system, key, rows and year. Always write AS.

Conversion Error: … can't be cast to the destination type STRUCT(…): comparing a STRUCT column to text, as in WHERE classification = 'Pathogenic'. Name the field: classification.name. See Reading a STRUCT column.

Binder Error: Referenced column "conditionQualifier" not found or schema mismatch in glob: reading proposition*.parquet without union_by_name = true. The four tables have different columns.

Text that prints \n: the DuckDB command line shows a newline inside a value as \n, so a list joined with newlines looks broken. The data is fine. Switch to .mode line to see the value as written, or join with '; ' instead.

HTTP 429 Too Many Requests: a remote query read too many row groups; see Local or remote.

items.title: Parquet for Previous Releases
items.text:
From release 1.2.0, only the current line (v1/1.2/) has published Parquet. A frozen line keeps its bundles and no Parquet (ADR 0008): the bundle is the record, and the tables are derived from it. This page shows how to build the tables of a frozen line yourself, with gkm-bundle-parquet 2.0.0 and a column set ClinVar-GKM publishes, so that you get compact tables and can prove that no value was lost.

Line Bundle schema_version Build its Parquet v1/1.1/ 1.1.0 with the 1.1.0 column set, on this page v1/1.0/ 1.0.1 not supported: build from the v1/1.1/ bundle of the same release; see The 1.0 line

These are the 2.0 tables, not the old 1.1 tables

gkm-bundle-parquet 2.0.0 writes table spec sections 2.0: one table per bundle section, 20 for a 1.1.0 bundle. These are not the 22 tables the 1.1 line published at v1/1.1/parquet/ (exported from BigQuery, with other names and columns), and queries written for those need rewrites; see Moving from the 1.1 Tables to 2.0. The tables differ from the 20 tables of the 1.2 line only where the 1.1.0 schema differs from 1.2.0.

items.title: Why a column set
items.text:
The tool generates a bundle's tables from its JSON Schema. With no column set, every property the schema allows becomes a column. The 1.2.0 schema narrows ClinVar-GKM's classes to what the pipeline writes, so its default is the published tables. The 1.1.0 schema leaves many classes as general as the GA4GH classes they extend, so its default is much wider than the data:

Built from the 2026-10-31 weekly delta (495,547 records) Top-level columns Leaf columns JSON-text columns 1.1.0 schema, generated default 339 553 122 1.1.0 schema, ClinVar-GKM's 1.1.0 column set 163 366 0

Both sets rebuild the same records. The default's extra columns are properties no 1.1 bundle holds (always NULL), and positions it keeps as JSON text because the schema leaves them open. The column set lists only the properties the 1.1 pipeline writes, each with a type.

The column set is a named projection (projection: clinvar-gkm-1.1.0-producer): the tool labels every file and the manifest with that name and the column set's sha256, so the tables can't be mistaken for the default. A projection could lose data if it left out a property a record holds, but in 2.0.0 that can't happen silently: the build stops on any record holding a property the column set doesn't list, naming the record. A build that completes kept every value, and the round-trip check below proves it record by record.

items.title: The 1.1.0 column set
